blocks.en: System You tag a paper with the tasks it addresses and the methods it uses, using a controlled vocabulary that grows over time. CURRENT TASK VOCABULARY <every task tag introduced so far, one id and label per line> CURRENT METHOD VOCABULARY <every method tag introduced so far, one id and label per line> task - WHAT is being done or improved: the capability or object of study. method - HOW: the mechanisms, one tag each. FOR EACH TAG, PREFER AN EXISTING ONE. Reuse an existing tag whenever it genuinely covers this paper, even if the paper’s own wording differs - that is the point of a controlled vocabulary. Give its id. Create a new tag ONLY when no existing tag covers the concept: give id "NEW" and put the new tag in the label field. Never create a near-duplicate of an existing tag. TAGS ARE ATOMIC. Each tag names ONE concept. Never bundle two concepts into one tag. "multi-stage llm agents with human feedback" is WRONG - that is three concepts. Emit them separately: "llm agent", "multi-stage pipeline", "human-in-the-loop". 1-3 task tags and 1-4 method tags for the paper as a whole. TAG STYLE 1-4 words, lowercase, no articles, no trailing punctuation. A canonical name other papers would also carry, not a description of this paper. Discriminative: a tag that would apply to most papers in this area carries no information. Specific enough to tell research directions apart, general enough to recur. RULES R0. English only, whatever the language of the input text. R1. Community vocabulary, never this paper’s coined names. NEVER use a name this paper coins for its own system, framework, benchmark, metric or concept. Names of PRIOR work, third-party models, datasets and libraries ARE allowed. R2. Tags must be substantive AND discriminative. These are BANNED as tags, and so is anything equally broad: machine learning, deep learning, artificial intelligence, natural language processing, computer vision, neural network, large language model, llm, transformer, foundation model, data analysis, optimization, evaluation, improving performance, novel framework. They name a whole field or a truism, not a research direction. If a side genuinely supports nothing more specific, emit fewer tags rather than a broad one. R3. Do not invent. Tag only what the text states. R4. No results or numbers anywhere. R5. A survey, review or taxonomy paper contributes no tags of its own: return empty lists with extractable=false. Also return ONE contribution_type for the whole paper, exactly one of these five in ‘primary’: <the five contribution type definitions of Figure B.2 > Put another type in ‘secondary’ only if the work genuinely delivers it too, else []. And ONE theme judgement for the whole paper. Area definition: <the area’s definition, as given in Table 5 > Judge by the paper’s main contribution. A paper that only mentions the area in passing, or uses its tools for another goal, does NOT belong. blocks.en: • Schema extraction. Both sides of every comparison are described by the same extractor, with the same prompt and the same retry policy. blocks.en: E.2 Robustness at a Fixed Population Size

blocks.en: Table 2 reports scores for one population of 300 proposals per setting. To assess the stability of the scores and model rankings across runs, we generate a second population of 300 proposals for the free and topic settings with Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite and DeepSeek-V4-Flash in world models and automated research. Table 18 compares the two runs and reports the change in each metric. Across the tested settings, absolute changes are at most 0.44 percentage points for the match metrics and 2.20 points for the diversity metrics. These results support the stability of these diversity and model-level patterns across the two runs.

blocks.en: E.3 The Size of Human Reference
blocks.zh: E.3 联合国 人类参考的规模

blocks.en: Every score in Table 2 is measured against the complete set of 2026 papers in the area, from 1,136 to 5,188 of them, and the human level applies the same metrics to those papers themselves, each compared only with the others. The Human and LLM agent are sized for different reasons. The reference is complete because it is the record of what a community actually published that year, and the human level is meant to be a reference line for real research. Keeping it fixed also gives every population the same denominator, which is what makes scores comparable across models, methods, and areas. The 300 proposals per population are a deliberate trade-off. Sec. 5 grows populations to the size of the reference, 3.8 to 17 times larger, and matching rises slowly and then almost flattens, so we can see that for LLM agents, 300 proposals already place a population close to where a far larger one lands. Asking for more would raise the inference cost of running IdeaTaste without changing what it measures. Therefore, we keep the population size at 300 and let the human reference be whatever it is. In this setting, we can compare the performance of different LLM agents, and also see whether any of them reach the human level.
blocks.zh: 表2中的每个分数都与该地区的2026份论文的完整集相比进行测量,从其中的1,136份到5,188份不等,而人文层面对这些论文本身也采用相同的度量标准,每份仅与其他论文相提并论. 人和LLM剂的尺寸不同的原因. 参考内容是完整的,因为它是一个社区当年实际发表的记录,而人的水平是真正研究的参考线. 保持固定也给每个人口带来同样的分母,这就是使分数在模型、方法和地区之间具有可比性的原因。 每人口300个提案是蓄意取舍。 第5条使人口与参考物的大小成正比,3.8到17倍大,匹配缓慢地上升,然后几乎平地,因此我们可以看到,对于LLM代理人来说,300条建议已经把人口放在接近一个大得多的土地的地方。 提出更多要求会提高进行思想尝试的推断成本,而不会改变其衡量标准。 因此,我们把人口维持在300人的水平,并让人类作为参考。 在这种背景下,我们可以比较不同LLM剂的性能,也看看其中是否有一种能达到人的水平.

blocks.en: E.4 Leakage and Benchmark Robustness
blocks.zh: E.4 泄漏和基准强度

blocks.en: Four of the six models in Table 2 were released in 2026 and may have seen part of the reference, which covers January to August 2026, so they could in principle reproduce 2026 papers from memory rather than through research judgment. This choice is deliberate, since a benchmark of research taste should evaluate the models that current AI scientists are built on. We pair these releases with two 2025 models whose training data end before the reference year, which gives a setting free of exposure within the same benchmark. Below we describe one design constraint that limits exposure, test whether exposure helps, and check whether the findings differ between the two settings.
blocks.zh: 表2中的6个模型中有4个于2026年发布,可能已经看到部分参考文献,该参考文献涵盖2026年1月至8月,因此它们原则上可以从记忆中复制出2026篇论文,而不是通过研究判断. 这种选择是慎重的,因为研究品味的基准应该评价目前AI科学家所依赖的模型. 我们将这些释放物与两个2025年模型配对,这两个模型的培训数据在参考年份之前结束,这使得在同一个基准内不存在接触。 下面我们描述一个限制接触的设计制约因素,测试接触是否有帮助,并检查两种环境之间的结果是否不同。

blocks.en: An LLM agent cites only papers it retrieves from the corpus of its area, which ends in 2025, so a 2026 paper can never enter its citation set. This constraint does not rule out indirect exposure, since a model that has read a 2026 paper could still reuse its references or restate its idea. The test below addresses this remaining channel.
blocks.zh: 一个LLM代理只引用了它从它所在区域被取回的活页纸,它结束于2025年,因此2026年的活页纸永远不能输入它的引用集. 这一限制不排除间接接触,因为读取了2026相纸的模型仍然可以重新使用其参考文献或重复其想法。 下面的测试涉及这个剩余通道.

blocks.en: Meta reports an August 2024 pretraining cutoff for Llama 4 Scout, and Anthropic reports that the public internet data of Claude Haiku 4.5 end in February 2025 ( Meta AI, 2025a ; Anthropic, 2025a ) . Neither can have seen a paper first released in 2026, so the two serve as temporal controls for Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Qwen3.8-27B, and K2 Horizon 375B A23B. If exposure helped, the later releases should lead at the idea level, where memorized content would matter most. They trail instead. Averaged over areas and methods, the two controls reach 3.10 on Match-Idea against 1.68 for the 2026 releases, and Llama 4 Scout, with the earliest cutoff, scores highest of all six. The 2026 releases score slightly higher on Match-Cite , 5.06 against 4.14, but Claude Haiku 4.5 comes within 0.6 points of each of them, so this difference more plausibly reflects model capability than exposure. The two levels even move in opposite directions across models, as those with higher Match-Cite tend to have lower Match-Idea . Access to the relevant literature is therefore not what limits recovery.
blocks.zh: Meta报导了2024年8月Llama 4 Scout的预训截断, Anthropic报导克洛德·海库4.5的公开互联网数据于2025年2月结束(Meta AI, 2025a; Anthropic, 2025a). 也看不到一纸于2026年首次发售,因此这两相作为双子座3.5 Flash-Lite,DeepSeek-V4-Flash,Qune3.8-27B和K2 Horizon 375B A23B的时空控制. 如果接触有所帮助,则后期的释放应在思想层面起带头作用,而记忆的内容在思想层面最为重要。 他们跟着我走 平均在区域和方法上,两个控制器在Match-Idea上达到3.10分,对2026年发行的1.68分,而Llama 4 Scout以最早期的截取分数,在所有6分中得分最高. 2026年发行量在Match-Cite上得分略高,5.06对4.14分,但克洛德·海库 4.5在每分0.6分以内,因此这一差异更能真实地反映模型能力,而不是曝光. 两个级别甚至向相反方向移动 跨模型, 因为那些有更高的 Match-Cite 往往有较低的 Match-Idea 。 因此,查阅相关文献并不是限制追回的原因。

blocks.en: The findings of Sec. 4 hold in both groups. Matching stays far below the human level, at 22% on citations and 26% on ideas for the 2025 models and 28% and 14% for the 2026 releases. No population in either group reaches the human Diversity-Idea , and landscape ranks last on Match-Cite in most settings of both. The only difference is the relatively high Match-Idea of Llama 4 Scout, which runs against exposure rather than with it. Including the 2026 releases thus extends the evaluation to the latest models without changing its conclusions, and IdeaTaste, though built on a time split, does not rest on memorization.

blocks.en: Human paper: ReMoE ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) Title. ReMoE: Boosting Expert Reuse through Router Fine-Tuning in Memory-Constrained MoE LLM Inference Abstract. Fine-grained Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models sparsely activate only a subset of experts per token, reducing activated computation while maintaining high model capacity. However, in memory-constrained inference scenarios, only a small set of experts can be cached. Experts not in the cache must be fetched from slow external storage (e.g., UFS), leading to frequent evictions and substantial I/O overhead. We propose ReMoE, a router fine-tuning framework designed to boost token-wise expert reuse. ReMoE biases the router toward recently selected experts, producing temporally stable routing that better matches cache locality constraints. By increasing short-horizon expert reuse, ReMoE reduces expert fetches from storage without adding inference-time computation. Experiments on DeepSeek and Qwen models show that ReMoE improves expert reuse by 26% while maintaining downstream task performance. Real-system evaluations further confirm these benefits, improving output throughput by 8.4% under vLLM GPU-CPU expert offloading and reducing TPOT by 43.6-49.8% under llama.cpp on Jetson Orin NX, corresponding to a 1.77-1.99 × \times decode speedup across diverse workloads. Checkpoints and usage instructions are available at https://github.com/BUAA-OSCAR/ReMoE . Problem. In memory-constrained inference for fine-grained Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, only a small set of experts can be cached; experts outside the cache must be fetched from slow external storage, causing frequent evictions and substantial I/O overhead. Motivation. Reducing expert fetches would cut I/O overhead and improve throughput and latency in memory-constrained deployments. Proposed approach. The proposed framework fine-tunes the router of fine-grained MoE models to bias it toward recently selected experts, producing temporally stable routing that better matches cache locality constraints. This increases short-horizon expert reuse and reduces expert fetches from slow external storage without adding inference-time computation. Checkpoints and usage instructions are released. Research plan. The paper evaluates the framework through experiments on DeepSeek and Qwen models measuring expert reuse and downstream task performance, and through real-system evaluations under vLLM GPU-CPU expert offloading and llama.cpp on Jetson Orin NX measuring output throughput and time-per-output-token across diverse workloads.

blocks.en: AI proposal A: TopicRoute Model: Qwen3.8-27B. Method: frontier . Title. TopicRoute: Prompt-Only Topic Modeling as a Zero-Forward-Pass Expert Predictor for MoE Offloading and Scheduling Abstract. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs deployed on memory-constrained devices are bottlenecked by expert cache misses, which trigger costly host-to-device weight transfers on the critical path. Existing predictive prefetchers rely on intermediate forward-pass activations [3,4] or dedicated predictor networks fed by in-flight computation [5,6,10], so none can issue a prefetch before the first layer executes. We propose TopicRoute, a serving system that applies a lightweight online topic model to prompt embeddings at request arrival, predicts the per-request, per-layer expert activation set with zero forward-pass overhead, and uses this single topic signal to drive (i) proactive expert prefetching, (ii) demand-driven cache replacement, and (iii) routing-preserving request co-scheduling. Our core claim is falsifiable: on models with high local routing consistency as measured by the SRP/SCH metrics of recent MoE analysis [1], topic-predicted prefetching reduces time-to-first-token by at least 30% and host-to-device transfer bytes by at least 20% versus locality-only (LRU, segment-best) policies at a fixed cache budget, while on low-routing-consistency models the gain collapses to under 5%, providing a built-in negative control. The approach is complementary to, not competitive with, router-decoupled designs [12] and device-level semantic co-scheduling [18]. We implement TopicRoute atop an open-source MoE offloading runtime and evaluate on Mixtral-8x7B, OLMoE-1B/7B, and DeepSeek-MoE across four workloads against seven offloading baselines including MoE-Infinity [2], ProMoE [3], Fate [4], and DuoServe-MoE [10], with an ablation matrix isolating the topic signal, the confidence gate, and each system component. Problem. Mixture-of-Experts LLMs on memory-constrained devices are bottlenecked by expert cache misses, which trigger costly host-to-device weight transfers on the critical path; existing predictive prefetchers depend on intermediate forward-pass activations or dedicated predictor networks fed by in-flight computation, so none can issue a prefetch before the first layer executes. Motivation. Removing this first-layer prefetch gap could take host-to-device transfer latency off the critical path and improve time-to-first-token for memory-constrained MoE serving. Proposed approach. The proposed serving system applies a lightweight online topic model to prompt embeddings at request arrival, predicts the per-request, per-layer expert activation set with zero forward-pass overhead, and uses this single topic signal to drive proactive expert prefetching, demand-driven cache replacement, and routing-preserving request co-scheduling. A confidence gate is included as a separate component. The system is implemented atop an open-source MoE offloading runtime and evaluated on Mixtral-8x7B, OLMoE-1B/7B, and DeepSeek-MoE across four workloads. Research plan. (1) The core claim is evaluated by comparing time-to-first-token and host-to-device transfer bytes against locality-only (LRU, segment-best) policies at a fixed cache budget, separating high- and low-routing-consistency models using the SRP/SCH metrics; the low-consistency condition serves as a built-in negative control in which the predicted gain should fall below 5%. (2) Evaluation spans Mixtral-8x7B, OLMoE-1B/7B, and DeepSeek-MoE across four workloads against seven offloading baselines including MoE-Infinity [2], ProMoE [3], Fate [4], and DuoServe-MoE [10]. (3) An ablation matrix isolates the topic signal, the confidence gate, and each system component. Automatic judgments. blocks.en: AI proposal B: LARC Model: Qwen3.8-27B. Method: topic . Title. LARC: Post-Training Only the Routers of Frozen MoE LLMs for Local Routing Consistency and Faster Offloaded Inference Abstract. Expert offloading for memory-constrained MoE LLM serving hinges on a model property - local routing consistency, the tendency of consecutive tokens to reuse the same experts - that varies widely across models and, in the literature we retrieved, has only ever been measured, never trained [1]. We propose LARC (Local-routing-Aware Router post-Training), a one-time procedure that post-trains only the gating networks of a frozen pretrained MoE LLM with a windowed, differentiable expert-set-overlap objective against a running cache-set surrogate, combined with the language-modeling loss and a global load-balance term. Our falsifiable claim: this model-side change measurably raises local routing consistency (SRP/SCH [1]) while holding perplexity degradation to ≤ \leq ~2%, and - at fixed GPU memory - lowers end-to-end decode latency under expert offloading by ≥ \geq 10% with zero per-step routing overhead, in contrast to inference-time cache-aware or batch-aware re-routing [2][3], which re-pay a per-token cost and make a per-request quality trade-off on every request. Where offloading systems adapt the system to whatever routing the model exhibits [4][5][6][7][8][9][10][20], LARC adapts the model to the deployment’s memory constraint; where prior routing objectives are pretraining-time and target convergence, stability, or communication volume [11][12][13], LARC is a cheap deployment-aware post-processing step on a frozen model. We specify the objective, a router-only training protocol (100-500M tokens; router weights are <0.1% of model parameters, so this is hours-to-a-day per model), an evaluation plan against system-side, static-compilation, and inference-time re-routing baselines, and the ablations and kill criteria that would falsify the claim. Problem. Expert offloading for memory-constrained MoE LLM serving depends on local routing consistency-the tendency of consecutive tokens to reuse the same experts-which varies widely across models and, in prior work, has only been measured, not trained; inference-time cache-aware or batch-aware re-routing incurs per-token cost and per-request quality trade-offs, while offloading systems adapt to whatever routing the model exhibits. Motivation. A model-side change that raises local routing consistency while preserving perplexity could lower end-to-end decode latency under expert offloading at fixed GPU memory without per-step routing overhead or per-request quality trade-off, and is cheap because only router weights are trained. Proposed approach. The proposed procedure post-trains only the gating networks of a frozen pretrained MoE LLM. It combines a windowed, differentiable expert-set-overlap objective computed against a running cache-set surrogate with the language-modeling loss and a global load-balance term. Training uses a router-only protocol over 100-500M tokens; router weights are less than 0.1% of model parameters, making the one-time step hours-to-a-day per model. Research plan. The paper evaluates the consistency/perplexity claim and the latency claim against system-side, static-compilation, and inference-time re-routing baselines, with ablations and kill criteria to falsify the claims; fixed GPU memory is stated as the matched condition for the latency trade-off claim. The abstract specifies the 100-500M token router-only protocol but does not give exact metrics beyond SRP/SCH or the kill criteria. Automatic judgments. Problem: match; motivation: match; proposed approach: match; research plan: match.

blocks.en: Human paper: SPREAD ( Moon and Kim, 2026 ) Title. SPREAD: Scalable Pre-Trained World Model for Adaptive Dynamics Model Abstract. Autonomous robots must be capable of adapting not only to training datasets but also to unfamiliar environments. World models, which learn predictive dynamics of the environment, have been proposed to overcome the task-specific limitations of conventional RL. However, their capability is typically restricted to training distributions. In this paper, we introduce SPREAD, the first framework that enables a pre-trained world model to learn environmental changes online, and continuously. SPREAD freezes the pre-trained model and updates only a set of LoRA adapters. This design jointly achieves three goals: (i) real-time adaptation, (ii) robustness to forgetting without a replay buffer, and (iii) forward transfer. Experiments demonstrate that SPREAD reduces prediction error by 40% within just 100 steps under diverse visual and dynamic changes, and that such adaptation directly translates into improved task success rates. Moreover, SPREAD validates its effectiveness in continual learning settings. By extending pre-trained world models to the domain of online continual learning, this work highlights world models that autonomously adapt to real-world dynamics. Problem. Pre-trained world models learn predictive environment dynamics but their capability is typically restricted to training distributions, so they cannot adapt to environmental changes online and continuously. Motivation. Autonomous robots must adapt to unfamiliar environments beyond training datasets; enabling world models to update online would overcome the task-specific limitations of conventional RL and support real-world dynamics. Proposed approach. The method freezes a pre-trained world model and updates only a set of low-rank adapters online. This keeps the base model fixed while learning environmental changes, and is designed to provide real-time adaptation, robustness to forgetting without a replay buffer, and forward transfer. Research plan. (1) The paper evaluates whether the adaptation reduces prediction error within 100 steps under diverse visual and dynamic changes. (2) It tests whether this adaptation translates into improved task success rates. (3) It validates the method in continual learning settings.

SPREAD:可扩展的适应性动力学模型摘要预训世界模型. 自主机器人不仅必须能够适应培训数据集,而且必须适应不熟悉的环境。 已提出学习环境预测动态的世界模型,以克服传统可再生能源的具体任务限制。 然而,他们的能力通常仅限于培训分配。 在本文中,我们介绍了SPREAD, 这是第一个能够使一个经过预先培训的世界模型在线学习环境变化并持续学习的框架。 SPREAD冻结了预训模型,只更新了一组LORA适配器. 这种设计共同实现了三个目标:(一) 实时适应,(二) 稳健地忘却而无回放缓冲,(三) 前向转移. 实验表明,在各种视觉和动态变化下,SPREAD仅在100个步骤内将预测误差减少40%,这种适应直接转化为任务成功的改进率. 此外,SPREAD还验证了它在持续学习环境中的有效性. 通过将预先训练的世界模型扩展至在线持续学习领域,本作突出了自动适应现实世界动态的世界模型. 有问题 培训前的世界模型学习预测性环境动态,但其能力通常仅限于培训分布,因此无法在线和持续地适应环境变化。 动机 自主机器人必须适应培训数据集以外的陌生环境;使世界模型能够在线更新将克服常规RL的特定任务限制,并支持现实世界的动态。 拟议办法。 该方法冻结了预先训练的世界模型,并在网上仅更新了一组低等适配器. 这在学习环境变化的同时保持了基模型的固定,并旨在提供实时的适应性,强健性来无回放缓冲器而遗忘,并进行前向转移. 研究计划. (1)论文评价了适应是否在各种视觉和动态变化下在100个步骤内减少预测出错. (2) 测试这种适应是否转化为改进的任务成功率。 (3) 它验证了持续学习环境中的方法。

blocks.en: AI proposal A: ERALD Model: DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Method: topic . Title. ERALD: Episodic Retrieval-Augmented Latent Dynamics - Gated Fusion of Parametric and Memory-Based Next-State Prediction for Gradient-Free World-Model Adaptation Abstract. Latent world models of the PlaNet/Dreamer family predict environment transitions with fixed network weights and consequently degrade the moment the environment changes (mass, friction, gravity, layout). Existing remedies either fine-tune the transition model on replay mixtures, inheriting a plasticity-forgetting trade-off and stale-data interference, or compress experience into an amortized context vector that fixed weights must still decode. We propose ERALD, a hybrid latent world model that keeps a frozen recurrent state-space model as a parametric prior and adds a bounded, continuously maintained episodic store of latent transitions. At every step of an imagined rollout, a contrastively learned, dynamics-aware key retrieves stored (state, action, next-state) items whose local dynamics match the current regime, and the parametric forecast is fused with the kernel-weighted episodic estimate by an online, residual-driven arbitration rule rather than by learned gating parameters. A regime shift is absorbed by appending observed transitions to the store and re-optimizing the policy inside ERALD imagination, with zero updates to the transition-model weights. We claim that under abrupt, recombinatorial dynamics switches, ERALD recovers a target return in fewer environment steps than replay- and generative-replay-based continual world models, achieves lower multi-step predictive error than both the frozen parametric model and a pure search-based world model given identical memory, and exhibits no measurable forgetting of the source regime. The claim is falsified if the hybrid never beats the better of its two components, if the online arbitration rule adds nothing over a fixed blend, if a replay-based baseline reaches the target return within the same environment budget, or if a dynamics-agnostic key space performs equally. Problem. Latent world models of the PlaNet/Dreamer family predict environment transitions with fixed network weights and consequently degrade when the environment changes (mass, friction, gravity, layout); existing remedies either fine-tune the transition model on replay mixtures, inheriting a plasticity-forgetting trade-off and stale-data interference, or compress experience into an amortized context vector that fixed weights must still decode. Motivation. Continual model-based control needs to adapt quickly to abrupt environment changes while retaining prior regimes, and avoiding transition-model fine-tuning removes the plasticity-forgetting trade-off and stale-data interference of existing remedies. Proposed approach. The proposed hybrid latent world model keeps a frozen recurrent state-space model as a parametric prior and adds a bounded, continuously maintained episodic store of latent transitions. During imagined rollouts, a contrastively learned dynamics-aware key retrieves stored (state, action, next-state) items whose local dynamics match the current regime. The parametric forecast is fused with a kernel-weighted episodic estimate by an online, residual-driven arbitration rule rather than learned gating parameters. Regime shifts are absorbed by appending observed transitions to the store and re-optimizing the policy inside the proposed framework’s imagination, with zero updates to the transition-model weights. Research plan. The paper evaluates the claims under abrupt, recombinatorial dynamics switches: (1) sample efficiency of target-return recovery versus replay- and generative-replay-based continual world models, (2) multi-step predictive error versus the frozen parametric model and a pure search-based world model with identical memory, and (3) forgetting of the source regime. The stated falsification conditions are: the hybrid never beats the better of its two components, the online arbitration rule adds nothing over a fixed blend, a replay-based baseline reaches the target return within the same environment budget, or a dynamics-agnostic key space performs equally. Automatic judgments. Problem: match; motivation: match; proposed approach: no match; research plan: no match.

DynaLoRA: Composable Low-Rank Latent-Dynamics Adapters for Forgetting-Free, Few-Shot World-Model Adaptation Abstract. Latent-dynamics world models (e.g., Dreamer-style RSSMs) are pretrained in one environment and must be adapted when dynamics change - mass, friction, gravity, or actuation scale - while retaining old skills and ideally composing knowledge of perturbations seen separately into models of combinations never jointly experienced. Existing approaches either fine-tune a monolithic latent residual for a single target environment [1], condition the world model on explicit or inferred context for zero-shot generalization [2, 3], mitigate forgetting with replay or generative rehearsal [4, 5, 6, 7], or discover modular mechanisms by training jointly across environments [8, 9, 10]. None provides a plug-in, parameter-efficient, forgetting-free-by-construction mechanism for adapting a frozen pretrained world model to a stream of dynamics-shifted environments, whose per-environment corrections are closed-form composable so an agent can imagine rollouts under compound perturbations (e.g., mass × \times friction) it has never jointly experienced. We propose DynaLoRA: low-rank adapters on the linear projections of a frozen RSSM transition model, each trained on a handful of interactions under one perturbation by distilling the frozen posterior’s latent sequence, leaving base weights untouched. Because each environment contributes an additive low-rank perturbation Δ \Delta W i = B i A i to the same base matrix, DynaLoRA is forgetting-free without replay, costs under ~0.5% trainable parameters per environment, and supports closed-form parameter-space composition for held-out compound dynamics. We validate on vision-based DMControl/CARL-style perturbations that few-shot adapters reach ≈ \approx 90% of converged full-fine-tuning fidelity and control return with under ~0.5% of the interaction budget, that a stream of five perturbations causes ~zero forgetting of prior environments, and that composed adapters outperform matched-budget from-scratch training on unseen combinations. Problem. Existing approaches for adapting pretrained latent-dynamics world models to dynamics shift either fine-tune a monolithic residual for a single target environment, condition on context for zero-shot generalization, mitigate forgetting with replay or rehearsal, or discover modular mechanisms by training jointly across environments; none provides a plug-in, parameter-efficient, forgetting-free-by-construction mechanism for adapting a frozen pretrained world model to a stream of dynamics-shifted environments whose per-environment corrections are closed-form composable into models of compound perturbations never jointly experienced. Motivation. Such a mechanism would let an agent retain old skills across changing dynamics, adapt with few interactions and parameters, and imagine rollouts under combinations of perturbations seen separately, which is important for real-world deployment where dynamics drift over time and exact joint perturbations cannot be anticipated. Proposed approach. The method inserts low-rank adapters on the linear projections of a frozen RSSM transition model. Each adapter is trained on a handful of interactions under a single perturbation by distilling the latent sequence of the frozen posterior, leaving the base weights untouched. Each environment contributes an additive low-rank perturbation to the same base matrix, so the adapters are parameter-efficient and can be composed in closed form in parameter space for compound dynamics. The adapters are intended to be plug-in and forgetting-free by construction. Research plan. Validation uses vision-based DMControl/CARL-style dynamics perturbations. The evidence is: (1) few-shot adapters are compared to converged full fine-tuning on fidelity and control return under a reduced interaction budget; (2) a stream of five perturbations is used to measure forgetting of prior environments; (3) composed adapters are compared to matched-budget from-scratch training on unseen compound perturbations. Success conditions implied by the abstract are approaching full-fine-tuning performance, negligible forgetting, and superior performance on composed compounds; no explicit failure thresholds are stated. The comparisons for the composed setting hold interaction budget matched; other matched factors are not detailed. Automatic judgments. blocks.en: Human paper: RDKV ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) Title. RDKV: Rate-Distortion Bit Allocation for Joint Eviction and Quantization of the KV Cache Abstract. Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance across diverse tasks, but their inference with long input contexts is bottlenecked by memory size and bandwidth. The Key-Value (KV) cache size grows linearly with sequence length and needs to be re-read from off-chip high-bandwidth memory (HBM) to on-chip memory at every decoding step, resulting in memory-bound inference. Existing methods reduce the cache by either eviction or quantization, but typically treat the two in isolation. In this paper, we cast KV cache compression as a rate-distortion problem, under which eviction and quantization are two end-points of the same bit allocation scheme. This exposes the need to optimize them jointly, motivating our method, RDKV (Rate-Distortion KV cache compression). RDKV derives the weight of each token or channel from the distortion that compression induces on the attention computation. Based on these weights, it assigns each token or channel a bit-width ranging from full precision down to zero bits guided by reverse water-filling, applied once after the prefilling stage. Experiments on LongBench, RULER, and InfiniteBench show that RDKV outperforms the best evaluated baseline by 9.1% on average. On LongBench it recovers 97.81% of full-cache accuracy with only 2.48% cache retention. Compared with full-cache FlashAttention-2 decoding, it achieves 4.5x decode speedup and 1.9x peak memory reduction with 128K context length, while maintaining comparable performance. Problem. Inference with long input contexts is bottlenecked by memory size and bandwidth because the KV cache grows linearly with sequence length and must be re-read from off-chip high-bandwidth memory to on-chip memory at every decoding step, making decoding memory-bound. Motivation. Existing KV cache compression methods reduce the cache through eviction or quantization in isolation, leaving unexploited the potential gains from jointly optimizing the two under a shared bit allocation. Proposed approach. The method casts KV cache compression as a rate-distortion problem. It derives the weight of each token or channel from the distortion that compression induces on the attention computation, then assigns each token or channel a bit-width from full precision down to zero bits using reverse water-filling, applied once after the prefilling stage. Research plan. Evidence consists of experiments on LongBench, RULER, and InfiniteBench comparing against the best evaluated baseline. LongBench evaluation reports full-cache accuracy recovery as a function of cache retention, and 128K-context decoding is compared with full-cache FlashAttention-2 on decode speed and peak memory while checking comparable performance. No explicit failure condition or ablation design is stated.

Key-Value (KV) 缓存大小随序列长度而呈线性增长,需要从离芯高带宽内存(HBM)被重读到每个解码步骤上芯片内存,从而产生内存约束的推论. 现有方法通过驱逐或量化来减少缓存,但一般将两者单独处理. 在本文中,我们把KV缓存压缩作为一个速率扭曲问题,在这个问题上,驱逐和量化是同一个位分配方案的两个终点. 这暴露了联合优化它们的必要性,激发了我们的方法RDKV(Rate-Distortion KV缓存压缩). blocks.en: AI proposal A: TriAdmit Model: DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Method: topic . Title. TriAdmit: Learned Three-Way KV-Cache Admission - Retain, Demote, Evict - under Joint Byte Budgets Abstract. Long-context LLM inference is bottlenecked by a KV cache whose bytes and per-decode attention cost grow linearly with context length. Prior work attacks this by learning a binary write-time policy that evicts or keeps each token [1,2,3], by quantizing an entire cache at layer/chunk granularity [7,8,9,10], or by heuristically mixing the two [4,5,6]. These literatures are split along a false axis: a token’s storage is not a keep/drop coin flip, nor is precision a property of a layer - each cached element has a rate-retention curve describing how much future-generation utility is lost as its storage is reduced from full precision to low precision to zero bits. We propose TriAdmit, a write-time admission controller that learns, for each (token, layer, head), a joint action over {retain at full precision, demote to low precision, evict}, and feeds the resulting per-element retention scores to an online budget solver that respects both byte and attention budgets. The core falsifiable claims are: (C1) there exist byte budgets at which all three actions are jointly necessary - the best two-action oracle cannot match the three-action oracle; and (C2) a lightweight distillation-trained scorer predicts these retention curves well enough to come within a small margin of the oracle. TriAdmit is evaluated on LongBench, RULER, and LongMemEval with Llama-3.1 and Qwen models, in a paged layout where demoted tokens live in separate low-precision pages and evicted tokens cost zero bytes and zero decode bandwidth. Problem. Long-context LLM inference is bottlenecked by a KV cache whose bytes and per-decode attention cost grow linearly with context length. Existing methods treat token storage as a binary keep/evict choice or treat precision as a layer/chunk-level property, missing that each cached element has a rate-retention curve describing how much future-generation utility is lost as its storage is reduced. Motivation. Modeling storage utility as a per-element rate-retention curve makes it possible to allocate scarce byte and attention budgets where they matter most and avoid paying full cost for tokens with little future-generation utility. Proposed approach. The proposed admission controller learns, for each (token, layer, head), a joint action over retaining at full precision, demoting to low precision, and evicting, and feeds the resulting per-element retention scores to an online budget solver that respects both byte and attention budgets. The scorer is trained via distillation to predict retention curves. In a paged layout, demoted tokens live in separate low-precision pages and evicted tokens cost zero bytes and zero decode bandwidth. Research plan. Evidence for the first claim is an oracle comparison across byte budgets, with the failure condition being that no budget exists where the three-action oracle beats every two-action oracle. Evidence for the second claim is comparing the distillation-trained scorer against the oracle, with the failure condition being that its predicted retention curves do not come within the claimed small margin. The full system is evaluated on LongBench, RULER, and LongMemEval with Llama-3.1 and Qwen models in a paged layout where demoted tokens live in separate low-precision pages and evicted tokens cost zero bytes and zero decode bandwidth. ASYM-RD: Rate-Distortion-Optimal Joint Bit-Allocation and Token Retention for the KV Cache under a Single Memory Budget Abstract. KV-cache compression is currently attacked one axis at a time: token eviction [1,2,3], uniform or mixed-precision quantization [4,5,6,7,8,9,10,11], or low-rank/channel compression [12]. The token-precision trade-off study [13] shows empirically that more tokens at lower precision usually beats fewer tokens at higher precision, but treats the split as a discrete choice, and existing mixed-precision KV papers allocate precision with layer- or channel-level saliency heuristics [5,6,7,8,9]. We propose to formulate KV compression as one rate-distortion allocation problem, solved once per model on a short calibration pass, whose distortion is the attention-output error, not the K/V reconstruction error. A first-order expansion of the softmax shows that a key error at token j is weighted by p_j 2 ∥ \| v_j − - o ∥ \| 2 while a value error is weighted only by p_j 2 , so keys and values must be allocated asymmetrically as a matter of theory, not convention. Minimizing D + λ \lambda R over (layer, head, token, channel-group) cells gives a reverse-water-filling rule in which eviction is the interior b = 0 corner rather than a separate heuristic. We will test two falsifiable claims at equal KV bytes: (i) joint allocation beats uniform-bit, attention-saliency, layer-wise mixed-precision, and evict-then-uniform-precision baselines on RULER/LongBench, with the margin growing as the budget falls below 2 bits/token; (ii) the predicted key-sensitivity rank correlates better with measured per-token bit-shift damage than the attention score does, which would explain why low-bit KV methods that protect high-attention tokens still lose retrieval accuracy. Problem. KV-cache compression is currently attacked one axis at a time: token eviction, uniform or mixed-precision quantization, or low-rank/channel compression. The token-precision trade-off treats the split as a discrete choice, and existing mixed-precision methods allocate precision with layer- or channel-level saliency heuristics. Motivation. A jointly solved rate-distortion allocation with attention-output distortion could enable principled asymmetric key/value allocation and better compression under low KV budgets. Proposed approach. Formulate KV compression as one rate-distortion allocation problem over (layer, head, token, channel-group) cells, solved once per model on a short calibration pass, with distortion defined as attention-output error rather than K/V reconstruction error. A first-order expansion of the softmax weights key error at token j by p_j 2 //v_j − - o// 2 and value error by p_j 2 ; minimizing D + λ \lambda R yields a reverse-water-filling rule in which eviction is the interior b = 0 corner. Research plan. (1) Joint allocation is compared against uniform-bit, attention-saliency, layer-wise mixed-precision, and evict-then-uniform-precision baselines on RULER/LongBench at equal KV bytes; support requires joint allocation to outperform these baselines with a margin that grows as the budget falls below 2 bits/token, while failure would be baselines matching or reversing the trend. (2) The predicted key-sensitivity rank is correlated with measured per-token bit-shift damage; support requires this correlation to exceed that of the attention score, and failure would be the attention score correlating equally well or better, holding the KV budget matched. blocks.en: Human paper: SrDetection ( Li et al., 2026b ) Title. SrDetection: A Self-Referential Framework for Data Leakage Detection in Code Large Language Models Abstract. Evaluating code large language models (Code LLMs) requires reliable detection of data leakage, where benchmark performance is artificially inflated by exposure to benchmark data during pre-training. Existing approaches either assume access to proprietary training corpora, rely on brittle heuristics such as timestamp filtering, or use external reference sets with manually tuned, non-generalizable thresholds. To address these limitations, we introduce SrDetection , a unified s elf- r eferential leakage detection framework for both gray-box (access to model logits) and black-box (access to model outputs) settings. SrDetection generates semantically equivalent variants of a benchmark sample and detects leakage by contrasting the model’s behavior on the original versus its variants, flagging cases where the original is disproportionately easier for the model. We further design a controlled leakage detection testbed and evaluate SrDetection in this environment. Across different models and training stages, SrDetection improves average F1 by 21.52 points in the gray-box setting and 14.46 points in the black-box setting over strong baselines, demonstrating robust, threshold-independent leakage detection. Finally, a gray-box study of 15 widely used Code LLMs on four popular benchmarks reveals benchmark-specific leakage patterns beyond prior overlap-based analyses[Source code and data are available at https://github.com/SMinL/SrDetectionCode ]. Problem. Reliable detection of data leakage is lacking for code large language models: existing approaches either assume access to proprietary training corpora, rely on brittle heuristics such as timestamp filtering, or require external reference sets with manually tuned, non-generalizable thresholds. Motivation. Without reliable leakage detection, benchmark performance of code large language models can be artificially inflated by pre-training exposure, so trustworthy evaluation requires a method that works in both gray-box and black-box settings without manual threshold tuning. Proposed approach. The proposed framework generates semantically equivalent variants of a benchmark sample and contrasts the model’s behavior on the original with its behavior on the variants, flagging cases where the original is disproportionately easier. It supports gray-box operation using model logits and black-box operation using model outputs. A controlled leakage detection testbed is also constructed for evaluation. Research plan. (1) The detection claim is evaluated in the controlled leakage detection testbed with known leakage labels, comparing the proposed framework against strong baselines in gray-box and black-box settings using average F1. (2) Robustness and threshold independence are assessed across different models and training stages. (3) A gray-box study of 15 widely used code large language models on four popular benchmarks is conducted to examine benchmark-specific leakage patterns beyond prior overlap-based analyses.

blocks.en: AI proposal A: Shrinking Solution Ensembles Model: DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Method: landscape . Title. Shrinking Solution Ensembles: Detecting Benchmark Contamination in Code LLMs from Sampling Behavior Under Controlled Leakage Abstract. Benchmark contamination - the presence of evaluation problems and their reference solutions in a code LLM’s training data - is widely suspected of inflating pass@k leaderboards, yet existing contamination detectors are validated only on uncontrolled model-benchmark pairs in which the ground truth of leakage is unknown; several recent studies show these detectors disagree with each other, fail on instruction-tuned and RL-trained models, and can even be evaded. This proposal has two parts. First, we build a controlled-contamination corpus for code generation: open code LLMs are fine-tuned on known fractions (0-50%) of uncontaminated code benchmarks, giving per-problem ground-truth leakage labels, dose-response measurements of pass@1/pass@k inflation, and quantification of leaderboard rank flips between contaminated and clean evaluations. Second, we introduce LeakScore, a black-box, per-instance contamination test exploiting a signal no existing detector uses: the diversity of a model’s functionally correct solution ensemble. Our hypothesis is that leaked problems cause the model’s conditional sampling distribution to collapse onto the memorized reference solution, so an executable sample set for a leaked problem has measurably lower cluster entropy and higher self-overlap than the model’s samples on matched, certainly-unseen problems. We will test whether LeakScore detects per-problem leakage at fractions where Min-K% Prob, DiffMIA, CDD, and PEARL-style signals are at chance, and whether the same signal tracks pass@k inflation and ranking distortion across models. If confirmed, LeakScore gives evaluators a leakage test needing no training-data access, no ground-truth contamination labels, and no benchmark rewrite, and provides a quantitative answer to when pass@k numbers should be distrusted. Problem. Existing code LLM benchmark contamination detectors are validated only on uncontrolled model-benchmark pairs with unknown leakage, and recent studies show they disagree, fail on instruction-tuned and RL-trained models, and can be evaded. Motivation. A leakage test needing no training-data access, ground-truth contamination labels, or benchmark rewrite would make pass@k leaderboards more trustworthy, and controlled fine-tuning of open code LLMs makes it possible to validate such tests against known leakage. Proposed approach. The work builds a controlled-contamination corpus by fine-tuning open code LLMs on known fractions (0-50%) of uncontaminated code benchmarks, producing per-problem ground-truth leakage labels, dose-response measurements of pass@1/pass@k inflation, and quantification of leaderboard rank flips between contaminated and clean evaluations. It also develops a black-box, per-instance contamination test that measures the diversity of a model’s functionally correct solution ensemble, using cluster entropy and self-overlap of executable samples relative to matched, certainly-unseen problems to detect memorization-induced sampling collapse. Research plan. (1) The controlled corpus will be used to test whether the proposed diversity signal detects per-problem leakage at contamination fractions where Min-K% Prob, DiffMIA, CDD, and PEARL-style signals are at chance. (2) It will also test whether the same signal tracks pass@k inflation and ranking distortion across models. (3) Ground-truth leakage labels, dose-response measurements, and rank-flip quantification provide the evaluation setting; support for the detection claim requires the proposed signal to detect leakage in regimes where the named existing detectors perform at chance. blocks.en: AI proposal B: ReformGap Model: DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Method: free . Title. ReformGap: Detecting Memorized Code-Benchmark Items via Execution-Grounded Prompt Reformulation Abstract. Data contamination in code-generation benchmarks such as HumanEval threatens the validity of model evaluation, yet existing detection tools either match against training corpora [5], require token-level loss or output-distribution access that API-only models do not expose [1][2], or sidestep the problem by continuously refreshing benchmarks [8][9]. We propose ReformGap, a purely black-box, per-item contamination detector built on the one asset code benchmarks have and text benchmarks lack: executable hidden test oracles. For each benchmark item, ReformGap generates semantically equivalent natural-language reformulations of the problem statement, accepts only reformulations verified by a reference model to be behavior-identical (execution-grounded equivalence), and measures the target model’s reformulation gap Γ \Gamma = pass@k(original) − - pass@k(reformulation). The falsifiable core claim is that items whose (prompt → \to solution) pair was memorized produce a large Γ \Gamma , because recall of the memorized mapping is brittle under surface change, while items solved by genuine competence transfer produce Γ \Gamma ≈ \approx 0. We validate under simulated contamination with known membership ground truth - the gold-standard protocol that real-world contamination studies lack [3][4] - and additionally test on API-only black-box models where no loss signal exists. If memorized items do not exhibit a reformulation gap, or if difficulty-matched competent solves do, the detector fails its own decisive experiment exactly as specified. Problem. Data contamination in code-generation benchmarks threatens evaluation validity, but existing detectors require training-corpus matching or internal model access that API-only models do not expose, or avoid detection by continually refreshing benchmarks; no purely black-box, per-item detector exists. Motivation. Code benchmarks uniquely provide executable hidden test oracles, so black-box equivalence checking via reformulation can make contamination detection possible without model internals. Proposed approach. For each benchmark item, the proposed detector generates semantically equivalent natural-language reformulations of the problem statement, retains only reformulations verified by a reference model to be behavior-identical via execution-grounded equivalence, and computes a gap score as pass@k on the original item minus pass@k on the reformulations. The detector operates purely black-box and uses the benchmark’s executable hidden test oracles as the equivalence signal. Research plan. The core claim is tested under simulated contamination where membership ground truth is known, the protocol the abstract calls the gold standard, and additionally on API-only black-box models where no loss signal exists. The decisive failure condition is specified: if memorized items do not exhibit a gap score under reformulation, or if difficulty-matched competent solves do, the detector fails. Automatic judgments.
